---
title: "Probabilistic Structures"
slug: v/latest/cache/structures
---

`cache.structures` gives you four tiny data structures that answer big questions with a few kilobytes: "was this seen before?", "how many distinct users?", "how often did this term appear?". They trade a small, known error for memory you can ignore.

```ts
import { cache } from "@warlock.js/cache";

const usernames = cache.structures.bloom("users.usernames", {
  expectedItems: 1_000_000,
  errorRate: 0.01,
});
await usernames.add("hasan");

if (!(await usernames.mightContain(input))) {
  // definitely free: skip the database lookup
}
```

They live on the cache manager (not on every driver) and are supported on **`redis`** and the memory drivers (`memory`, `memoryExtended`, `lru`). Any other driver throws `CacheUnsupportedError`; custom drivers need no change.

Every structure takes `ttl` (a number of seconds or a string like `"40d"`). It is set when the structure is first written and is not pushed back by later writes, so `"1h"` gives you a window that ends an hour after its first event.

Keys follow the driver's `globalPrefix`, and the structures are stored apart from your plain keys (`structures.<kind>.<key>`).

## Bloom filter: "definitely not" or "probably yes"

```ts
const filter = cache.structures.bloom("users.usernames", {
  expectedItems: 1_000_000,
  errorRate: 0.01, // default
});

await filter.add("hasan"); // true when it was not (probably) there before
await filter.mightContain("hasan"); // true
await filter.mightContain("nobody"); // false means it was never added
```

`false` is always right. `true` is wrong `errorRate` of the time.

| Items     | Error rate | Memory  | Hashes |
| --------- | ---------- | ------- | ------ |
| 1,000,000 | 1%         | ~1.2 MB | 7      |
| 1,000,000 | 0.1%       | ~1.8 MB | 10     |

Good for: username-taken checks, a shield in front of lookups for random ids, blocklists, "already sent this email?".

Not for: anything where a wrong "yes" is unacceptable (permissions, payments), or sets you need to shrink or list. You cannot remove an item or list the contents; use a cuckoo filter if you need removal.

Add far more than `expectedItems` and the error rate climbs; size it for the growth you expect.

## Cuckoo filter: membership with removal

```ts
const banned = cache.structures.cuckoo("users.banned", { expectedItems: 100_000 });

await banned.add(userId);
await banned.mightContain(userId); // true
await banned.remove(userId); // true when something was removed
await banned.mightContain(userId); // false
```

Same promise as the Bloom filter, plus `remove`.

:::caution Only remove what you added
Removing an item that was never added corrupts the filter and can make other items disappear. Remove only what you know you added, once per add.
:::

With RedisBloom this is a real cuckoo filter. On every other backend it is a counting Bloom filter: the same API and error rate, with a small counter per position instead of a bit, so memory is larger (a hash on Redis). `remove` returns `false` without touching anything when the item clearly was not added.

## Unique counter: how many distinct values

```ts
const dau = cache.structures.uniqueCounter(`stats.dau.${today}`, { ttl: "40d" });

await dau.add(request.user.id);
await dau.count(); // approximate number of distinct ids

// Union across counters without changing them
const week = await cache.structures.uniqueCounter.merge(lastSevenDaysKeys).count();
```

A HyperLogLog: about 12 KB per counter and a standard error of 0.81%, whether you count a thousand or a billion. Counting the same value again changes nothing. `merge` counts the union, so a week is the distinct users across seven daily counters (someone active every day counts once).

Not for: "did user 42 visit?" (it cannot tell), and not for billing, which needs exact counts.

On Redis this is the native `PFADD` / `PFCOUNT` / multi-key `PFCOUNT`.

## Frequency: how often, and what is most common

```ts
const searches = cache.structures.frequency("search.terms.hourly", {
  width: 2000,
  depth: 5,
  topK: 100,
  ttl: "1h",
});

await searches.add(query.toLowerCase()); // or add(query, 3)
await searches.estimate("laptop"); // never lower than the true count
await searches.top(10); // [{ value: "laptop", count: 120 }, ...]
```

A Count-Min sketch plus a Top-K list. With `width: 2000, depth: 5` it uses about 40 KB. It only ever **over**-estimates, and by at most about 0.14% of all events seen, 99.3% of the time. `topK` (default 10) is how many leaders are remembered for `top()`; `top(n)` returns up to that many, highest first.

Not for: rare values. A value seen a handful of times can be swamped by the overestimate; use it for the head of the distribution.

## What runs where

| Backend                              | Bloom, frequency, cuckoo                 | Unique counter          |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Redis with RedisBloom                | native `BF.*`, `CF.*`, `CMS.*`, `TOPK.*` | native HyperLogLog      |
| Redis without it                     | bitmaps, hashes and a sorted set         | native HyperLogLog      |
| `memory`, `memoryExtended`, `lru`    | in process                               | in process              |
| `file`, `pg`, `null`, `mock`, custom | `CacheUnsupportedError`                  | `CacheUnsupportedError` |

Redis checks once for RedisBloom (with `MODULE LIST`) and remembers the answer; if the command is refused it uses the portable path. Switching between the two on an existing key is not supported: they store data differently. In-memory structures are per process, follow `flush()` and `removeNamespace()`, and vanish on restart.

On the portable Redis path each add is a few commands, not one atomic script; it stays correct under concurrency because every step only sets bits or adds to counters.

## Writing your own driver support

A driver opts in by implementing one method:

```ts
import type { CacheStructuresBackend } from "@warlock.js/cache";

class MyDriver extends BaseCacheDriver<Client, Options> {
  public structuresBackend(): CacheStructuresBackend {
    return new MyStructuresBackend(this);
  }
}
```

`CacheStructuresBackend` is a small set of primitives (bit set/get, counter grids, distinct counts, a ranked list); the structures are built on top of it, so you do not reimplement hashing or sizing.
